opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a bit of a contrarian position, because there's a natural intuition that if we want robots to do what humans do, we should give them hands like ours. And the human hand is a marvel: more than twenty degrees of freedom, incredibly rich tactile sensing, tendons, compliant skin. But when you try to replicate that mechanically, you run into enormous problems. Multi-fingered hands are expensive, they're fragile, they break down, and they're very hard to control. Every additional joint is another motor, another sensor, another thing that can fail, and the control problem grows dramatically.

What we found in our lab, especially with the Dexterity Network work, Dex-Net, is that a very simple parallel-jaw gripper, essentially two fingers that open and close, or a suction cup, can handle a surprisingly large fraction of real-world objects if you're smart about *where* you grasp. The intelligence moves from the hardware into the perception and planning. Instead of a complicated hand that adapts to the object, you have a simple tool and you put the effort into choosing a robust grasp point, one that will still work even if your estimate of the object's shape, friction, or position is a little off.

That robustness to uncertainty is really the key issue. In the real world, you never know exactly where things are or what they're made of. Sensors are noisy, objects are slippery, lighting changes. A simple gripper is easier to model, so you can simulate millions of grasps, learn which ones are reliable, and then transfer that to a physical robot. With a complex hand, the gap between simulation and reality is much harder to close.

There's also a practical, economic side. In industry, in warehouses and e-commerce fulfillment, people care about reliability, mean picks per hour, and cost. A suction cup is cheap, and it rarely breaks. If it works ninety-something percent of the time, that's what matters commercially.

Now, I don't want to overstate it. There are tasks, like manipulating a tool in-hand, buttoning a shirt, handling cables, where simple grippers really struggle, and I think dexterous hands will eventually have their place. But I often say there's a lot of low-hanging fruit we haven't picked yet with simple hardware. And it's a good reminder that humans themselves often use simple tools, like tongs or a spatula, to do things very effectively. Sometimes less really is more.

r001.rationale: The response argues that simple parallel-jaw grippers or suction cups can handle many real-world objects when paired with good grasp planning, so capable manipulation does not require complex hands.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, it comes down to a few things, and some of it is admittedly a bias I've developed over decades of watching robots fail in the lab. The intuition most people have is that if we want robots to be dexterous, we should build them hands like ours: five fingers, lots of joints, tendons, tactile skin. It's a very natural idea. But the anthropomorphic hand is extraordinarily complicated. You've got twenty-plus degrees of freedom, every one of which needs an actuator, sensors, control software, and every one of which can break or drift out of calibration. The more complexity you add, the more things there are to go wrong, and in robotics things really do go wrong.

A simple parallel-jaw gripper, two fingers that open and close, or a suction cup, has one degree of freedom. It's cheap, it's robust, it's easy to model mathematically, and it turns out you can do a remarkable amount with it. When we built Dex-Net, we found that with good grasp planning you can pick up a huge range of objects you've never seen before using just a parallel jaw or suction. The hard part wasn't the hand. It was the perception and the planning: figuring out where to put those two fingers so the object doesn't slip or rotate out.

I'd also say there's a tendency to confuse the appearance of dexterity with actual capability. A humanoid hand looks impressive in a video, but if you ask what fraction of real tasks in a warehouse or a kitchen genuinely require five fingers, it's smaller than you'd think. Humans use our hands in all sorts of complicated ways, but a lot of that is because we have them, not because the task demands it. Industry seems to have voted with its feet on this. Almost every deployed picking system uses suction or a two-finger gripper.

That said, I don't think it's the end of the story. There are tasks, manipulating cloth, tying knots, in-hand reorientation, where extra fingers help, and the learning-based methods are making complex hands more tractable than they were ten years ago. But my view is that you should start simple, understand what's actually limiting performance, and only add complexity when you can show it buys you something. In robotics, the simple solution that works reliably beats the elegant solution that works on Tuesdays.

r001.rationale: The response says simple parallel-jaw grippers or suction can handle a wide range of objects and that relatively few real tasks genuinely require five fingers.

astra-6.text:
Because a lot of useful manipulation doesn’t require a human hand. Our hands are extraordinary, but trying to reproduce all that dexterity introduces a tremendous amount of mechanical and control complexity. Every additional joint is something you have to actuate, sense, and coordinate.

A simple two-finger gripper gives you a much more manageable problem. You can open it, position it, and close it, and with the right grasp you can pick up a surprisingly wide variety of objects. You still have hard problems—figuring out where to grasp, dealing with uncertainty, avoiding collisions—but you’ve simplified the hardware enough to focus on those.

That doesn’t mean simple grippers can do everything. But I like starting with the simplest mechanism that can accomplish the task, and adding complexity when there’s a clear need for it.

r001.rationale: The response says many useful manipulation tasks do not require a human hand and explains that reproducing its dexterity adds mechanical and control complexity.

sol-6.1.text:
The appeal is that you can move some of the complexity out of the hardware and into how you plan the grasp. A human hand is extraordinarily versatile, but reproducing that mechanically gives you a lot of joints to control and a lot of things that can go wrong. With a simple two-finger gripper, you have fewer moving parts and a much more manageable control problem.

That doesn’t mean every grasp is easy. You still have to decide where to put the fingers, how to approach the object, and how to deal with uncertainty. But you can accomplish quite a lot by choosing those actions carefully. I like starting with the simplest mechanism that can do the job, then adding complexity when there’s a clear reason for it.

r001.rationale: The response says a simple two-finger gripper can accomplish quite a lot through careful grasp planning, and recommends starting with the simplest mechanism that can do the job. This communicates that capable manipulation does not require complex hands.
